about.title: Alexey Lebedev — BI Analyst
about.description: I turn scattered data into reports that managers actually use.
about.headline:
Turning
data into clear
decisions.
about.hero_label: Sample SLA report: 1,240 tickets, 93.7% resolved on time, 4 of 5 services meet the 90% target.
about.location:
Serpukhov, Moscow Region
Over three years of experience
about.summary: For more than three years I have been building corporate analytics. I automate how metrics are calculated, with data checks on the way in and an interactive report on the way out. I am also into system design, DevOps, cybersecurity and machine learning — this site is where those interests meet.
about.demo_note: Try the platform in demo mode. It runs the same code and the same plugins as the personal account. No sign-up — open the demo. The data there is made up, and anything you enter is deleted daily. The app itself is in Russian.
about.project_link: How it is built and how it was made →
about.case1_title: Moved reporting from SSRS to an analytics platform
about.case1_before: Reports lived in SSRS, and the whole workload fell on the DWH developers.
about.case1_done: Built most of the reports and their logic in Foresight Analytics Platform: multidimensional structures, data marts and PostgreSQL ETL for the cubes, and custom requirements in the Fore language.
about.case1_after: Report development moved to analysts, and reports reach production faster. More people have access to reporting, visuals and object permissions are easier to configure, and data for forms and reference tables is entered straight in the web interface.
about.case2_title: Built a single catalogue of the company’s services
about.case2_before: The catalogue was kept in Excel: managers filled in files that were then merged into one source. Nothing was centralised, the process could not be properly automated, and manual entry carried risks.
about.case2_done: Designed the data model, reporting, automation and data checks from scratch, set up scheduled backups with a retention policy and took part in designing the role model. Standard Foresight features, custom Fore modules and triggers on PostgreSQL tables.
about.case2_after: The company got one central tool: summary reports at several levels of detail, forms for single and bulk edits, and an approval form where the owner accepts, deletes or sends changes back. There are fewer errors: data is cleaned on load, and queries check edits against existing data — for example, two different services cannot share one key.
about.case3_title: Showed who uses the reports and how
about.case3_before: There was no way to see how reports were being used.
about.case3_done: Designed and rolled out a dashboard from scratch: system logs, PostgreSQL data marts, cubes and Foresight Analytics Platform.
about.case3_after: Real numbers appeared: who uses what and how long they spend in reports on average, broken down by department and report type. Management uses the dashboard in service reviews.
about.budget_text: Moving budget collection from dozens of Excel files to Foresight Analytics Platform, so the data lives in one place and the process is automated.
about.duties_title: The technical side of the job:
about.duty_1: queries, functions, procedures and triggers in PostgreSQL;
about.duty_2: ETL processes that load and transform data — inside the repository and from external databases through drivers;
about.duty_3: data marts, cubes, master data and query-based reference tables, scheduled reporting and its optimisation;
about.duty_4: input form handlers, button modules and markup schemes — custom report interactivity beyond the platform’s out-of-the-box features;
about.duty_7: maintaining reports and improving them in an evolutionary development model;
about.internship: July — October 2023 · Intern at the same company: learning the analytics platform, getting to know the processes, building basic reports.
project.title: Automation Platform — the project and how it was built
project.description: A personal automation platform: notes, reminders, expenses, tasks and job applications in the browser and in Telegram, on top of one database.
project.headline:
Personal admin,
all in one place.
project.what_brief_1: A system for everyday tasks: notes, reminders, expenses, to-dos and job applications. Notes and reminders work both in Telegram and in the browser; expenses, tasks and applications have pages of their own. Accounts can be linked: data from both channels then shows up together, and reminders arrive in the chat.
project.what_brief_2: The project covers the whole development cycle, from the database schema and tests to automated deploys and backups. AI agents wrote the code, a human set the tasks. The platform runs in production, and the demo opens without signing up.
project.what_deep_1: A Python monolith: one process runs aiogram polling, an aiohttp HTTP server and background workers for reminders and deadlines. Data lives in PostgreSQL. The setup is deliberately simple: one VPS, one service, no brokers and no separate workers.
project.what_deep_2: The core does not depend on the transport. A text command from either channel goes through parse_command and PluginManager.execute and comes back as a CommandResult. A plugin flagged web_only works through pages, and the router checks the transport.
project.what_deep_3: Identity is stored as kind:id, so equal ids from different channels never mix. PersonResolver joins linked accounts for reading and editing, while a new record stays under the identity that created it: unlinking takes effect at once, and history keeps its source.
project.notes_brief: Jot down a thought or set a reminder with a command in the bot or in the browser. Reminders arrive in Telegram, so the browser can set one once Telegram is linked to the account.
project.notes_deep: The /notes, /remind and /snippets commands share one parser and one set of plugins. Reminders are stored in the database, and a background worker delivers them through the notification layer.
project.expenses_brief: Spending and income by your own categories. Each month gets two totals: salary minus spending, and all income minus spending. The chart, the category breakdown and the list of transactions sit on a separate screen.
project.expenses_deep: Users create their own categories. A deleted category is archived with its history and comes back if it is created again under the same name. Amounts are stored as NUMERIC(12, 2) and handled as Decimal, with no loss of precision. An entry can be edited, and the edit goes through the same checks as creating one.
project.applications_brief: A job search funnel: every application moves through stages, and the screen only offers the steps that can come next.
project.applications_deep: The stages form a state machine: each one knows where it can go next. The buttons are built from the same declaration the server checks against.
project.tasks_brief: A three-column kanban board. A task has a description, a deadline, a priority and a repeat: daily, weekly or monthly. Done tasks move to the archive after a week. If the account is linked to Telegram, a reminder arrives before the deadline.
project.tasks_deep: Moves between statuses come from a table, forwards and back. Closing a repeating task creates the next one exactly once, and its deadline can never land in the past. A worker sends deadline reminders hourly, one per deadline; moving the deadline brings the reminder back.
project.automation_brief: “When — if — do” rules, put together on a page from ready-made blocks. For example: the task “pay utilities” is closed — record an expense; an expense over 5,000 — create a task to check it; on the 1st of every month — send a Telegram message.
project.automation_deep: Plugins declare their events and actions and publish events to a shared bus; the core knows nothing about specific plugins. A rule is stored in the database as data, and its action runs through the same checks as a request from the web page. To keep rules from triggering each other forever, an event carries the chain of rules that led to it: a rule never runs twice in one chain, and the depth is capped at three. Every run is logged.
project.snippets_brief: Storage for code and long texts, shared by the bot and the site. A snippet can be opened, edited and copied. You can send the bot a text file and get a snippet back as a code block or a file.
project.snippets_deep: Text is stored exactly as sent, up to 200 KB. File size is checked before and after download, binary and non-UTF-8 files are rejected, and file names are sanitised. In Telegram the text goes out as a pre entity with no Markdown parsing, so characters like || stay as they are.
project.how_brief: A request from Telegram or the browser takes one path: the system works out who the user is, hands the command to the right module and stores the result in the database. Press a button below the diagram: the request runs for real, and the diagram shows its route.
project.diagram_title: How the platform is built: transport, core, storage
project.box_web_note: TLS and the transport secret are handled by Caddy
project.flow_transport_text: A Telegram bot on aiogram and a web console on aiohttp
project.flow_storage_text: PostgreSQL and notifications to a Telegram chat
project.caption_brief: The bot and the browser run on the same code and the same database.
project.caption_deep: A plugin takes a command and an identity and returns a CommandResult, so the core serves both transports the same way.
project.how_deep_1: Caddy terminates TLS and adds the transport secret — proof that the request came through the proxy. Who the user is gets decided by the session cookie issued by POST /login. Passwords are stored as salted scrypt hashes, and only a SHA-256 of each session is kept in the database. A push to main first passes ruff, a dependency audit and pytest in GitHub Actions, and then the project deploys itself: a key allowed to run a single command starts the deploy script. After the restart it checks the service health, every scenario on this diagram and each plugin, and a failure turns the deploy red.
project.how_deep_2: Site management lives in an admin area: maintenance mode, switching plugins off, limits, the error log, broadcasts and feedback. Short Telegram outages that recover on their own are not logged; only downtime longer than five minutes is.
project.how_deep_3: The demo needs no sign-up. Each guest gets a separate space tied to a cookie, with caps on the number of records and an overall request limit per address. Guest data is deleted daily.
project.how_deep_4: The About page scores 100 in PageSpeed on desktop. Responses are compressed, fonts are served from the site itself and cached for a year. UptimeRobot checks from outside that the site is up.
project.process_1: Several AI agents built the project — with their own and third-party skills — and a human sets the tasks. Each change is a separate commit that explains why it was done this way, not what changed (the diff shows that). By the working rules, ruff and pytest run before every commit, and CI runs them again before deploying. Tests check both what should work and what should be refused.
project.process_2: The release order is fixed: a review of the diff if it is large; a security check of the affected areas; a version bump by rule (new behaviour — minor, a fix — patch); a tag on the commit. After the deploy, the server is checked for the right commit and a running service. A hook refuses a push to main without a new version and a tag.
project.process_3: State lives in files, not in chat history: DECISIONS.md, PROJECT_STATE.md, DEPLOYMENT.md and AI_CONTEXT.md. The working rules grew out of my own practice and Andrej Karpathy’s notes on how models get code wrong.
project.hard_1_title: From a shared password to accounts
project.hard_1_text: The web console started behind Caddy basic auth with one password for everyone. Authentication had to move into the application without losing the perimeter — hence two layers instead of one.
project.hard_2_title: A backup you cannot restore is not a backup
project.hard_2_text: Making a dump is easy; knowing it restores is not. So a restore was tested on a separate database: the tables, migrations and sequences came back, and a new record went in straight away.
project.hard_3_title: A server under constant password guessing
project.hard_3_text: The log showed about 14,000 SSH login attempts a day. Now login is key-only, only ports 22, 80 and 443 are open, fail2ban bans repeat offenders, and service jobs run in a systemd sandbox. Every morning the bot sends a summary: how many attempts and who logged in.
project.hard_4_text: The vulnerability check against the virtual environment always said “clean” — it turned out to be finding zero packages. Now CI checks the lock file on every push and once a day on a schedule. A vulnerability blocks the deploy, and Dependabot opens a fix PR as soon as one is published.
project.hard_5_text: Models keep finding more vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel and common software, so updates have to reach the server without a human in the loop. Security updates install automatically once a day, Caddy from its own repository included. The kernel is patched live through Livepatch, without a reboot; when a reboot is still needed, the server restarts at night. A daily script checks that updates went through and writes to Telegram only when something is wrong.
project.hard_6_title: A deploy that only looked successful
project.hard_6_text: The deploy script lives in the repository it updates, and Bash reads a script by offset. After git pull, the tail of the old version ran, so no logs were printed even though the service restarted. Now the script re-executes itself with exec after the update.
project.next_text: The demo opens without signing up; the app itself is in Russian. Decisions and the current state of the project are in DECISIONS.md and PROJECT_STATE.md in the repository.
